analyze_text: YPFS: Describe what you did during the crisis of 2007-09 as Deputy Director of Insurance and Research. Diane Ellis: My responsibilities were managing the FDIC Deposit Insurance Fund and its risk-based pricing system and related deposit insurance fund activities. I also had responsibilities for the research function. I also played a pretty big role in implementing our Temporary Liquidity Guarantee Program because the person I worked for, Art Murton, the Director of the Division of Insurance and Research, was involved in the very early stages and participated in meetings during Columbus Day Weekend in 2008 in with Treasury and the Federal Reserve to design this program. He had responsibility for implementing it, and since I was his deputy, it became my purpose as well. YPFS: Had you any background in designing and implementing such a program? Diane Ellis: No, none of us did. The guarantee part of it was very foreign to us. Or foreign enough. Obviously, insuring deposits and guaranteeing debt, you can see some similarities between them, but there were enough differences and important differences that we were having to really learn on the fly. YPFS: Were you at the agency during the Savings and Loan Crisis? Diane Ellis: I started in 1988, so yes. I was in California at the time as a young bank examiner. Things started to fall apart in California in about '89, about a year after I had joined. I was a bank examiner examining troubled savings and loans and banks at that time. Reasonably large institutions, by standards back then. Now, they wouldn't be considered all that large, but they were large at the time. I was in a boots-on-the-ground role rather than a policymaking role, but yes, I had some familiarity with troubled institutions. YPFS: Could you draw on that experience during the financial crisis of 2007-09 or was it very different? Diane Ellis: In some ways, but it was different. The banking crisis of the late 1980s and early 90s was a much slower developing credit problem. It moved geographically from one region of the country to another and while it was collectively a big problem, it was a more traditional crisis as banks and thrifts made a bunch of bad loans that weren’t repaid and the banks and thrifts ran out of capital and had to close. The systemic implications were completely different in 2007-09, a crisis that hit the big banks so quickly and with such ferocity and led to the freezing of markets and had serious implications for the real economy. It initially felt very different from the savings and loan crisis. YPFS: Was the FDIC and your group at the agency involved from the get-go or did you get drawn in as the crisis unfolded? Diane Ellis: What do you mean by the get-go? YPFS: When issues started surfacing in 2007 with BNP Paribas. Diane Ellis: My group wasn't involved quite that early. The group that would have been brought in first would have been our examiners, who would have been examining banks, such as when there was the Bear Stearns problem. Bear Stearns had some insured depository institutions, so supervisors were brought in from that perspective. While the examiners were starting to get drawn in here and there, as an agency we weren't playing a major role in 2007. It wasn't really until IndyMac failed in July of '08 that we realized we had a big resolution problem on our hands. We had a reasonably sized institution that we weren't prepared to resolve because it failed so quickly. We had to put it in conservatorship for a while and our resolution specialists were all occupied doing that. It was such a hit to our deposit insurance fund that our deposit insurance fund was getting close to insolvent. To me, that's the event when the FDIC really got involved. Even then, it wasn't until the fall that my group, in particular, got pulled in. YPFS: Your group was responsible for developing the TLGP wasn’t it? Diane Ellis: In terms of the policy development piece of it, we were the leaders. But it was an agency-wide effort. We couldn't do it all by ourselves. We needed some bank supervisory help on this. We had to pull in the lawyers and the people who handled the accounting functions, too. YPFS: Talk about the process of coming up with the TLGP program. Diane Ellis: I was not involved in the discussions with the other agencies, the Treasury and the Federal Reserve and so forth. There was a small group that met on Columbus Day weekend with the other agencies that included our Chairman, Sheila Bair, Art Murton, our acting general counsel at the time and maybe one of her advisors. It was a very small contingent brought in to discuss this issue, so they were involved in the back and forth of determining the very high-level outline of this program. The Treasury and the Fed reached out to us and said the U.S. needs a debt guarantee program and we think the FDIC needs to be the one to guarantee the debt. It was a decision that was determined by outside agencies and left to us to manage. Our folks came back after Columbus Day weekend and said, “We're basically guaranteeing all this debt right now and we've got to figure this program out." That's when I got involved. I was trying to figure out: What is this we've got on our hands now? YPFS: The FDIC was asked to get involved because it had the ability to invoke the system risk exception, correct? Diane Ellis: Right, that was certainly the authority. My understanding is that other countries, including the U.K., had already adopted or implemented their own versions of debt guarantee programs and the thinking of high-level policymakers in the U.S. was that our banks needed a similar program as well. That's what led them to the FDIC because we had the systemic risk exception authority and, also, we had the resources to cover the expense of the program. YPFS: People cite the TLGP as key to bringing about stability in the financial markets. Would you agree with that? What was it about the program that was so essential? Diane Ellis: The evidence is that it worked. We had a situation in which for quite some time banks weren't issuing any debt at all, which was very unusual. They started issuing in significant amounts when we got this program right and the program eventually led to narrowing spreads and so forth. We now see, based on the evidence, how helpful it proved to be. TLGP was part of a package of programs announced over Columbus Day weekend in 2008 that worked in concert. There was the TARP program. That represented the point at which the regulators switched from the idea that relief would be provided in the form of an asset-purchase program to a capital-injection program. Then there was the Federal Reserve’s Commercial Paper Funding Facility. And the TLGP. It was a very strong action by the authorities to bring the crisis to an end. It worked. And the FDIC definitely played a very critical role by helping to unlock the debt markets, which were utterly frozen up at the time. When we initially published our interim-final rule, the banks didn't do anything. There was no take up. Banks were not issuing debt, and we had to ask some of the industry participants, "What's wrong here?" We heard we were treating the debt relief as if it were insurance and we were treating the incidence of default like a bank failure. We had proposed to come in, resolve the bank debt, put the bank in receivership, sort through the expenses and determine the priority claims and then give the banks their money. The advice from industry participants was: The FDIC needs to be a guarantor and that is different than an insurer. A guarantor steps in and makes timely payments of principal and interest. That was a big leap for us internally because it was so different from the role we play in terms of providing deposit insurance. The way we had structured the program initially, there was no guarantee that they were going to get their money right away. I can't remember what we said about that, but I know in our mind we were thinking, "Well, okay, they'll default. We'll sort through things and figure it out." It was understood there would be no timely payment of principal and interest. Eventually, we structured it as a true debt guarantee. If there were a default, we would guarantee timely payment of principal and interest. The guarantee was backed by the FDIC, which has the full faith and credit of the U.S. behind it. YPFS: Was everybody on board with the new program structure? Diane Ellis: I remember there was a lot of internal turmoil. The lawyers were concerned about making a payment without having protected ourselves and without an ability to recover. When a bank fails, we get a subrogated claim and we have claims to all the assets that are available. We worked with an outside counsel to figure out how to, as best we could, ensure that we had some sort of legal claim on the assets of the company that had defaulted. We went back to the drawing board, figured out the problem of timely payment of principal and interest, went out quickly with a notice-and- comment rulemaking and responded with a final rule right around Thanksgiving. When we put that final rule in place there was a big rush on the part of the banks and holding companies to issue debt. YPFS: What allowed Europe to be a first mover on the debt guarantee front? Was it the way their financial regulators are structured? What did you learn from the Europeans’ experience? Diane Ellis: I don’t know. It always surprised me. It may be because they were dealing with fewer and very large banks. YPFS: Did you study their institutions and how they structured agreements and draw on that? Diane Ellis: We did. I made a couple of phone calls trying to get some tips on how they had structured things and I remember, in particular, talking to them about how they were pricing the guarantee. They based the pricing on credit-default swaps because they only had a single-digit number of banks, all who issued credit-default swaps. We had trouble with that. We were dealing with thousands of institutions and we only had a small fraction of banks that issued credit default swaps. We wanted the program to be available to our entire industry. YPFS: Talk about how the program was structured. It was in two parts, right? Diane Ellis: Yes, there were two parts. What the Fed and the Treasury wanted us to do was just guarantee debt. Frankly, they probably would have been happy if we had just guaranteed the debt at the largest companies. But our Chairman, Sheila Bair, said no. Her argument was if you're going to give the big banks something, we're going to make that opportunity available to all institutions, regardless of whether they have access to these kinds of markets regularly or not. Then, too, she's the one who advocated for the Transaction Account Guarantee (TAG) program because she knew the smaller institutions would benefit the most from that. We had heard plenty anecdotally about corporate treasurers taking money and any uninsured funds out of banks to put it in so-called, “too- big-to-fail” institutions. From a political perspective, it was a brilliant move. I don't know whether she was thinking about this at the time or not, she probably was, but in retrospect there was something for everyone in that program. The small banks weren’t going to complain about the big banks getting the debt guarantee program because they got their own program. It eliminated any resistance on the part of community banks. If it had just been a debt guarantee program, all those small community banks would have been up in arms and there would have been much more political resistance to the program than there was. YPFS: Describe in more detail the two components of the TLGP program. Diane Ellis: The Debt Guarantee Program is the one that gets the most attention. We knew that we’d be guaranteeing senior unsecured debts. But we had to figure out exactly what we were guaranteeing and what we were not guaranteeing. We knew it would be 125% of newly issued debt on banks’ balance sheets. Again, Sheila Bair resisted guaranteeing debt that had already been issued. Giving people who had already made decisions to invest in debt some sort of windfall wouldn’t be right, so it was agreed that it would just be newly issued debt that was guaranteed to get the banks to start issuing debt. Guaranteed debt issuance was capped at 125% because we wanted participants to be able to roll over existing debt and allow room for some growth. Pricing was another matter. Some people would have liked the program to be free but Sheila Bair determined we would charge a fee. At first, we settled on 75 basis points. We ended up abandoning the 75 basis points because it turned out that for anything that was short-term or overnight, such as fed funds, 75 basis points was way too expensive and yet it was not expensive enough for longer-term loans. We eventually priced guarantees on short-term debt at 50 basis points, 75 basis points for medium-term, and 100 basis points for long-term. We protected ourselves by making sure we had claims to the defaulting assets and we made all the banks sign a master agreement. Under the master agreement, in the event of a default, the FDIC got subrogation rights to go to court and make a claim. Outside of that, there were just a lot of reporting requirements. YPFS: Tell us about the TAG, or Transaction Account Guarantee, program. Diane Ellis: That was a lot simpler for us to wrap our heads around. That was not a very big leap in our thinking or our procedures. Aside from the accounting and having to segregate how much we charged for TAG and the extent of the losses we incurred and separating that accounting-wise from our normal deposit insurance premiums, there were no significant changes we had to make. We were just guaranteeing non-interest-bearing transaction accounts on an unlimited basis to reassure corporate treasurers that had large uninsured funds in banks. Both programs, I should mention, were voluntary. YPFS: What was the hardest part of implementing the programs? Diane Ellis: One of the harder thigns to do was figuring out what to guarantee, what constitutes senior unsecured debt. Is it federal funds? Is it euro dollars? What kind of debt is it? Were we going to guarantee debt with special features or should it just be plain-vanilla debt? Going through the entire right-hand side of a bank balance sheet and scrutinizing everything between deposits and capital and asking ourselves: ‘Are we guaranteeing that? Are we guaranteeing this?’ YPFS: What was the fallout from those choices? Diane Ellis: We cast a very wide net and basically ended up guaranteeing everything in between deposits and capital except subordinated debt or secured debt. I'm not sure we needed to do that. One of the lessons I learned is that once you guarantee a bank's longer-term debt, people are willing to lend to it short-term automatically. We probably could have kept the process a little simpler and made our lives a little easier if we said we are guaranteeing plain-vanilla senior unsecured debt and nothing else. It would’ve made reporting and recordkeeping simpler. Another way we could have made our life easier was not to have provided guarantees on commercial paper. We could have just done the long-term stuff. Commercial paper issuers expect to be paid the very same day and we had to work with someone at the Richmond Fed and the Treasury to set up procedures to get the money moved to the right place in case of a default. That was really hard. We were bombarded every day with questions about what kinds of debt we were guaranteeing, and again, I would keep that simpler next time. We were working with the rating agencies. That was frustrating. They were the ones saying, ‘You've got to demonstrate same-day payment capabilities for commercial paper or we're not going to rate this triple-A,’ which was really annoying. YPFS: Yes, especially interesting given the role they played in getting us into the crisis. Diane Ellis: We were thinking that. We're in this mess because of the triple-A ratings you slapped so willingly on sub-prime mortgage-backed securities, but yet, we, who have the full faith and credit guarantee of the government can't get a triple-A unless we demonstrate to you we've got the protocols to make same- day payments. Oh, it was really frustrating. YPFS: Did you have enough bodies on the ground to deal with this? I keep hearing from other agencies that they really had to staff up and draw people in from other places to help manage. Diane Ellis: Until we got things up and running, it was all-hands-on-deck and taking up a lot of resources from all over the FDIC. But, this program didn’t become an ongoing burden that required permanent staffing or even temporary staffing changes. We needed more people to close banks and to supervise banks and so forth, but not to run the TLGP. Institutionally, we were having to learn a lot about how the largest banks in the country funded themselves. Prior to the crisis, the FDIC historically had been more community bank-focused because of our supervisory and resolution responsibilities there. Getting involved in the intricacies of some of this was new. Now that we have some expanded authorities for dealing with the systemically important institutions, we're a lot more knowledgeable. YPFS: Central to the FDIC’s role was the systemic risk exception mechanism. Talk about how that authority led to the FDIC’s involvement in resolving the crisis. Diane Ellis: As an agency, it felt like we were being brought in a little late. Other regulatory agencies came to the FDIC and urged us to invoke the system risk exception and do the debt guarantee program. Policymakers were saying ‘You’ve got to do this debt guarantee program. You have the authority to do this. This is what the U.S. needs. This is what the G7 countries already have. It was thrust upon us. That's when I think Sheila said, ‘Well if I'm going to do this, this is what I want: I want to limit the guarantee to only new debt, I want the TAG, and so on.’ I wasn't in those conversations with Sheila, so I may not be the best source. This is where Art Murton might be a better source. But that's certainly the feeling I got and think most FDIC staff around would have. YPFS: What were the biggest concerns moving ahead with this? Diane Ellis: It was a double-edged sword atmosphere. One concern was we wouldn't get this right and no banks would issue debt and it would be a failed program. That was scary. That's why it was a big problem for us when we put the first interim-final rule out and nobody took us up on it. Nobody was issuing debt and they pointed out this timely payment problem. We knew we had to fix that right away. We didn't want to be responsible for a failed bailout program. The other thing we were really worried about was a major default. We were putting the rest of the banking industry on the hook for this. According to the systemic risk authority, if there is a loss, then the entire industry has to step up and pay enough to recover that loss, so if we are going to guarantee debt by Citicorp and Citicorp fails, we would have had to have every bank down to the $50 million bank pay for it. That would have been pretty awful. YPFS: Then, there was the issue of the deposit insurance fund losing money. Diane Ellis: A systemic risk exception, according to the law, was to be accounted for separately from the deposit insurance fund. Now, the deposit insurance fund was running out of money anyway, so it's not like there were a lot of resources directly there, but the systemic risk exception says if you lose money on that action, then you have to impose a special assessment on the industry to recoup those losses. It would have been accounted for a little differently or separately, at least. YPFS: When you saw the deposit insurance fund showing a balance of negative $20 billion, what was going through your mind? Diane Ellis: That was an uncomfortable feeling because, until then, all the problems had pretty much been in the largest banks. It was one bailout after another, but at the largest systemically important institutions. The deposit insurance fund was being used to resolve the smaller, more medium-sized banks, but they were actually failing. They were not being bailed out, they were failing. The fund was being depleted and if the fund was going to run out of money and we needed to go to Treasury, which we have the authority to do to get additional funds, the concern was, wait a second, now they're going to get painted with the bailout brush. The community banks at that point in time were on the moral high ground and they were screaming to be differentiated from the largest banks. We imposed a special assessment once to try to prevent the deposit insurance fund from going negative and the community banks were really unhappy about that. We had plans in place to impose another special assessment to prevent the fund from going negative, but that first special assessment ended up being equivalent to the entire industry’s earnings that year, so we decided we couldn’t do a second one. There weren't enough earnings to impose another special assessment, so we threw in the towel on and decided the fund would have to go negative. We still had enough liquidity to resolve things because there's a difference between solvency and liquidity, but then we started to get worried about that. All the liquidity we had was getting tied up in failed bank assets, so we needed liquidity. Again, we have the authority to go to the Treasury and borrow and we had done it in the early 1990s, but again, Sheila Bair came up with a different solution. She said, No, we're not going to do that. The industry can pay for this itself.’ Her reasoning was there was a lot of bailout fatigue at the time, and the industry was flush with cash because of all the monetary stimulus and so we should ask it to prepay assessments. It won't hit earnings and capital because it's a prepayment, and we can get the cash we need to continue to resolve banks seamlessly, without ever having to go borrow from the Treasury. Again, another brilliant move. YPFS: The FDIC is regularly described as being in a unique position to have helped resolve the crisis. Why is that? Is it the SRE authority? Diane Ellis: The FDIC is the only open-bank-assistance authority around because of the SRE. Going hand-in-glove with that authority is the resource issue. We can invoke the authority to provide the open bank assistance, but then if we suffer a loss, we have a claim on all the capital and earnings of the banking industry. If we exhaust that, we can go to the Treasury because we've got the full faith and credit guarantee of the U.S. government. We have authority and resources. YPFS: Let’s circle back a minute on the deposit insurance fund dipping into negative territory. Was that alarming? Or not, because you knew it would be temporary? Diane Ellis: Normally, we like to be able to inspire confidence. To inspire confidence, we would like to be able to point to a nice-sized deposit insurance fund and say, ‘See, we've got all these resources, not to worry, your money's safe because it's insured and we have the ability to pay you if there's a failure.’ During the crisis, it didn't feel good. We thought, ‘Oh, gosh, this will not be very inspiring when the press jumps all over the fact that we've got a negative fund balance.’ You get worried about creating a panic. But, by then, we were closing banks left and right every week and seamlessly providing funds and making good on that guarantee. Interestingly, in a time of crisis, it didn't cause panic because we were making good on our guarantee every Friday with more than one bank at a time sometimes. YPFS: The FDIC was one of the agencies that received pretty good press during this period, it seems. Diane Ellis: That's true. Sheila Bair was on the outside of the Geithner, Paulson, Bernanke trio and she was a bit of a thorn in their sides, but I think she got good press and goodwill as a result of it. She was challenging them and she had good sensibilities about what the people really wanted and needed and cared about. We got good press and I think she deserves a lot of credit for that. YPFS: You mentioned that since the crisis, the role of the FDIC has been expanded. Can you speak to that? Diane Ellis: Yes, it's the enhanced resolution authority: Title I and Title II of Dodd-Frank. Now, we receive and review and grade living wills for the largest institutions to hopefully get them in order to go through bankruptcy. If that doesn't work, we have the Title II authority, the ability to resolve not just the bank, but the entire bank holding company and its affiliates. It’s a big deal because we aren't just community-bank focused. The community banks are still a big deal to us because that's what most of our examiners do, but now we have more staff on site working side by side with the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the Federal Reserve and the largest institutions, so our access to information is much better than it used to be. We have more interaction with those institutions. In the past, there weren’t a lot of reasons for us to sit across the table from any of those firm's CEOs, but now there are. YPFS: Was there resistance to expanding the authority of the FDIC? Has there been pressure from this administration to shrink its role? Diane Ellis: There was a lot of vocal opposition to it right after Dodd-Frank but that's disappeared. The Mnuchin Treasury came out with a report early on that supported Title II, so that silenced some of the opposition. YPFS: The living will is simply a bank’s plan outlining how it intends to wind down its operations in bankruptcy? Diane Ellis: It's the preferred option. Ideally, we would like these large institutions to go through bankruptcy and the living will's the roadmap to get that done. YPFS: What had been going on before? Diane Ellis: Prior to the crisis, we thought that if one of these large institutions got into trouble, we at the FDIC would take the banking organization. Let's go back to Citicorp, as an example. In the past, if Citicorp were to face problems, the FDIC would take Citibank and resolve it using our normal tools. The rest of its affiliates and the holding company would proceed through bankruptcy court. When Citicorp got into trouble in the last crisis, we suggested we would take Citibank under our control and were told that wasn’t an option because the bank was too interconnected with the holding company and affiliates and couldn’t be chopped up. YPFS: If Lehman hadn't been left to fail, would things have unfolded differently? Did the FDIC have a position on whether Lehman should have been allowed to fail? Diane Ellis: If Lehman had not failed, everything would have unfolded very differently. We did not have a position on whether it should have or not because we've never taken a position or gotten involved in what's going on in the non-bank sector. We observe the sector and we monitor it because it matters, but we don't take policy positions over how non-banks should be handled. Lehman seemed separate from us. Now, we realize, well, maybe it wasn’t quite as separate as we thought. At the time, the press would refer to investment banks as banks. Morgan Stanley was a bank, Goldman Sachs was a bank. They were not banks. Yet, as it turned out, they were all banks in substance. Without Lehman's failure, I don't think there would have been any Columbus Day-weekend-need-to- intervene and there would be no TLGP and so on. Maybe there would be no Dodd-Frank or certainly no Title I and Title II rule. YPFS: Where are we now? What has changed for the better and what maybe hasn't changed that might be of a concern should we have another crisis? Diane Ellis: If the same crisis were to happen again, we'd be a lot smarter this time. Unfortunately, a crisis probably won't happen exactly that same way. We're ready to fight the last crisis, for sure. We would certainly be able to do things far more orderly now. We have more knowledge, more insight, more tools, to do things in a more orderly fashion. There is a contingent of folks that thinks our wings have been clipped a bit too much. There is now a big obstacle to tackling a crisis in that we would have to go to Congress to get authority to act. YPFS: You didn't need to do that before? Diane Ellis: No, we did not need to do that. Once we invoked the systemic risk exception and all the different keys had been turned, we were free to go and guarantee however much we wanted to. We had lots of freedom to design programs. Now, we will have to seek permission from Congress. YPFS: Is that required under Dodd-Frank? Diane Ellis: Yes. YPFS: Do you see any signs of a crisis in the making? Diane Ellis: Rapid growth and concentrations in an area generally is what leads to a bubble and the bursting of a bubble. With the exception of the leverage-loan area, we aren't really seeing anything worrisome on bank's balance sheets. The leverage loan area has experienced rapid growth and lots of deterioration in underwriting standards; that's a classic set up for a problem, but the numbers just aren't as big as they were in the mortgage market during the crisis of 2007-09. On top of that, there's not the same degree of derivatives transactions and so there's not a magnification of that credit risk. Also, there’s no impact on money market funds, whereas what made the subprime mortgage crisis so deadly was that it seeped into the money markets and overnight funding and so forth. I don't think we're repo-ing collateralized loan obligation debt and so I don't think it has a possibility of leading to the systemic freezing up of credit markets. YPFS: What are the biggest lessons that you learned in your role during the financial crisis? Diane Ellis: One of the biggest lessons for the FDIC was the interconnectedness. I think we were living in our own little world of insured depository institutions and thinking that all the problems and risk is in the non-banks. I gained an appreciation of how everything really comes back to the banks. YPFS: Thanks, Diane.
research_question: How did the FDIC design and implement the Temporary Liquidity Guarantee Program to stabilize American financial markets during the financial crisis?

analyze_text: YPFS: All right. We are officially recording. I'm Vincient Arnold. We have Greg Feldberg and Jason Cave. We are officially recording. Jason, are there any types of disclaimers that you want to make at the outset? Jason Cave: Well, now as a retired government employee, these are definitely my views and not the views of any former agencies where I worked. YPFS: Since this is a narrative history project, can we start out with a brief description of your role and capacity working at the FDIC during the global financial crisis? Jason Cave: Sure. I think about the beginning of the crisis as the Bear Stearns funds blowing up [in the summer of 2007]. I was running the FDIC's capital markets group, and that was mostly dealing with securities and interest rate risk, liquidity issues that our institutions—these would've been the community banks, state non-member banks—issues examiners and banks were running into. We were spending a lot of time at that time on Basel II. That was a big topic at the agency, so I was part of the group there working through the internal models and some of the concerns associated with that, which was taking a lot of time at all the agencies. Some have said maybe we were spending more time on that than we should have been, and maybe we should have been focusing on other things, and I'll leave that for others. But we were all spending a lot of time looking at securitization tranches and coming up with really low risk weights for highly rated tranches and putting a lot of effort into that. I was spending a lot of time there when it hit. YPFS: At that time, what was still needing to be resolved with Basel? Basel II came out in 2004. Jason Cave: Well, that’s a good point. What was going on at that point was really the US agencies, at least at the FDIC, had a strong hesitancy. We had had a relatively new change in our leadership. George French, who was a long-term research executive at FDIC in our deposit insurance area, moved over to policy, and that included the Basel work. And he had a lot of skepticism about the internal models and some of the capital requirements coming out of it. What you had was really the US—which had in some ways pushed for this new approach— we were the ones having a bit of cold feet. Everybody else had done it. We were spending a good amount of time around then putting in floors, convincing the Fed and others that were skeptical of putting in floors, that we really needed to have some check against some of the risk weights.3 So, a lot of attention in those years were on the US finalizing the US implementation. That seemed at the time to be heretical, putting in safeguards and standardized approaches, because at that time, the country and the world had seemed to decide—"models are good for risk management." They were like, "why are we bringing in all these other safeguards?" It seemed a little crazy. I think as the crisis played out, it was viewed as pretty prescient to have those backstops. And now these safeguards are not viewed as crazy. At that time, they were, and so we had to spend a lot of time debating with the Fed and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency [OCC] and the [banking] institutions. A lot was going on in those last innings. YPFS: I think that there was a misunderstanding and still is about Basel II, the fact that it had been implemented by investment banks in the US, but not actually by banks. Jason Cave: Right. YPFS: In 50 words or less, how come it hadn't been implemented in the US yet? Jason Cave: Fifty words or less—because we did a QIS, Quantitative Impact Study, that showed significant drops in capital when you apply the internal models unconstrained to mortgages, in the area of 80%. Some big drops. And so why it had not been implemented was that once we had really seen that, it gave everybody some significant pause. And so, the view was, "stop, let's get this right." Once we started to see those types of numbers, I think it gave the FDIC the support we needed with the other agencies to slow down. Then once you add all that to it, I think the [banking] institutions then were saying, "Why are we doing this again? We were spending all this money [on our models to justify lower risk-weights,] just to come up with a hundred percent risk weight. Gee whiz." So yeah, you had that, but you're right on the investment banks. That was back before the Financial Stability Oversight Council, and everybody was doing their own thing. The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) was tied in with the Brits and equivalents, and so you had an entirely different group doing it, and there you go. The rest is history. Wachovia and the First Proposed Ring-Fencing Arrangement YPFS: Let's talk a bit about Wachovia and Citi's bid for Wachovia. There was a ring-fencing arrangement proposed between the FDIC and Citi for the proposed acquisition of Wachovia. What can you tell us about that ring- fencing arrangement and how the FDIC got involved in it? Jason Cave: Sure. So, backing up just a bit, the FDIC, with the work of the other agencies, but mostly the FDIC, had just successfully closed the Washington Mutual (WaMu) deal Thursday night. It was a big deal. We had time to prepare. JPMorgan took it, no losses to the FDIC, some losses for some bondholders at the bank level, but we felt very good. It was very stable. Then we didn't have much time to celebrate when all of a sudden Wachovia [was under pressure]. People were taking future stress losses and bringing them forward to today. Now, the issue with that, with any leveraged institution is, if you do that, you're going to have a problem. And so, Wachovia was another one that folks like Paul Miller and others were saying, "Well, if you take all those losses..." And so, Wachovia was in the news, but we had focused so much on getting the WaMu transaction done that we hadn't spent a lot of time looking at Wachovia. All of a sudden Friday we get a call from the OCC that Wachovia is on the ropes, and it set off a pretty frantic weekend. I was actually at a wedding in Maine for most of it. I spent most of it outside of places like Gritty McDuff's, trying to do transactions with Bill Dudley and John Dugan and Sheila Bair and all that. It was pretty crazy. I want to be clear. It was not like it was out of the blue, but all of a sudden, the concerns seemed more immediate and pressing than perhaps we had thought. There was not just the fact of its size. I think there were a lot of discussions going on at different agencies and the FDIC really needed to get caught up like, "Where are we and what happened?" So that set off a very, very busy weekend. A lot of calls between principals and executives at Wells, Wachovia, Citi, asking, "What do we have here?" And a lot of people are not showing all their cards. There's a lot of information asymmetries and that sort of thing, where it seemed like during the weekend it was becoming clear that Wachovia was not going to survive on its own. That was becoming pretty clear by Friday night, Saturday morning, that as an organization it had to be closed—which was viewed as pretty extreme and a serious thing—that somebody was going to have to take it over. The real question was, will it be able to be done purely on a private basis or was there going to need to be some government assistance? And I think that was really where a lot of people were spending their time. We get into Sunday night, I get off the plane from Maine and I take a cab right over to FDIC because everybody else was already there. Sunday night was pretty crazy, seeing all of your colleagues in their weekend clothes, pretty stressed out with pizzas. It was like a war room. We're up on the sixth floor, the chairman's office, and there's Sheila and a couple of her people, and then Jim Wigand, Deputy Director of Franchise and Asset Marketing, Division of Resolutions and Receiverships, the receivership people and supervision, and they're working the calls with the OCC and Fed. It's sort of like you would picture it would be in a movie, how the movies would make it look. It was very tense, trying to get a sense of, "What do we have in front of us? How is this going to work?" And the beginnings of the outlines of a deal, a deal that was, again, based on [the view that] Wachovia on its own was not going to make it. We started to get a better sense [that] Wachovia was a different animal than WaMu. WaMu was a pure credit play with depositors that were getting nervous. They were beginning to run. You know, a traditional [run]. Wachovia is when we started to [focus on] the importance of the Asian markets opening and having a story about more runnable types of liabilities. I would say we were all learning that there were more runnable liabilities at Wachovia than possibly we knew, meaning investors that, whether it was 2a- 7 [money market] funds or the asset-backed commercial paper or financial commercial paper, that there was more of that than maybe, I think, everybody knew. I would have to say that I don't think people, at least, people at the FDIC, knew how much, what I would call very short-term credit-sensitive funding there was. Now, I don't really know what the number was. It became one of those things. It was just that it existed. There was not a lot of, "It's 50 billion in these funds that have to roll." We didn't have that information. Whether the New York Fed or Richmond Fed or others had it, I don't know. If they did, it wasn't shared. But you have to remember, we were in the fog of war, there wasn't that [information]. People were asking for it, but it wasn't available [to us]. You could take it two ways. You could say, "Was [the information] not available? Or was it available to the Fed, and they saw it was only $2 billion?" People would say, "Why are we getting involved?" The other issue is I think sometimes too, in those situations, even if the number was small, the FDIC management was like, "Yeah, but where do things go from here?" And so, we were kind of always dealing through the crisis with the problem that all of a sudden, even if it was $3 billion, you got the sense that the FDIC wasn’t really going to take any risks. Wachovia was a good example of the risk tolerance. YPFS: Because they're worried about the impact on the market and other banks who had similar funding? Jason Cave: Yeah. And so, it's one of the interesting things we do with data and information, we spend a lot of time. Now we're getting better information, but you sort of wonder. Okay, so even if we had perfect information and it was $3 billion, was Geithner going to say, "No"? Sheila probably would've said, "I'm definitely not doing anything for that." It's this interesting thing about how better information [may or may not help]... I think it's important, but it'll be interesting to see in a situation going forward if all of a sudden people are like, "Well, now we know it's only $2 billion that's got to roll tomorrow. We're good." We're not. Anyway. YPFS: Was one of the things discussed just supporting that market, or was it too early to talk about that? Jason Cave: It was too early. YPFS: It didn't come up? Jason Cave: No, no. It was still at that time there were different- YPFS: They had supported some markets already. Jason Cave: Right. There was some [talk about market wide support], but it was also like that's going to be too involved. That's going to be too complicated. We have this clear and present situation here that we have to deal with. YPFS: You talk about information gaps, but the FDIC always had backup supervisory authority. Jason Cave: Yeah. YPFS: To what extent was the FDIC not allowed information or hadn't been involved in Wachovia's issues for the previous couple of years? They could have been, because the FDIC was the insurer and it had the legal ability to do it. How did you feel about that before and after the crisis? Jason Cave: A good question. Fortunately, we had at that point some on-site presence. In fact, the examiner-in-charge there was a guy, Robert Burns, who was probably one of our best examiners throughout the crisis. He could really size exposures and provide good advice. He was sounding the alarm for at least a year ahead of time, you know, the Money Store trend.4 I would say we were well aware of the credit, the left-hand side [asset side of the balance sheet] problems at Wachovia. What I think we were not as aware of, and I think we all kind of learned, was just how the right-hand side [liabilities] could go so quick. I think that's the thing. If you looked at the old notes, [Robert] was doing everything he needed to do to raise the issues. It was that the fuse was a lot shorter than I think a lot of people realized. And so really, Sunday was the point, I think, where all the government was starting to get all the cards on the table and say, "This is what we know. This is what's going on." It became clear that someone, and I don't know who, pitched the idea of a ring- fence, because this would've been the first time, at least in the US. I think I had mentioned that UBS had done a ring-fence when they were running into problems. I don't know whether it was a month or six months [before Wachovia], but UBS, when they ran into their issues, the Swiss came up with this concept of, we need a ring-fence where the government is telling the market, "We got at least the tail, if not lower, coverage on this certain book of assets." In other words, to give the market some comfort, "We've got this." This idea had been done there, and I think that provided some people [comfort] just this idea of, "Hey, why don't we try something like that over here?" Whether it was at the Fed, or whether it was at Citi, or whether it was at Wachovia, I don't know, or maybe just investment banks. So that weekend, this concept of [a ring-fence] to be able to get Wells or Citi to the table to take Wachovia off our hands on an open basis—as an open bank thing—the idea was that we need some coverage from the government. In other words, if we're going to do it, we'll put in a bid, but it has to also be conditioned upon you guys [the government] also being on the hook for some amount of losses, which was unfortunate because there was a view that we might've been able to avoid that. But it did not matter whether on Friday or Saturday the view was that we, the government, could avoid [covering some of Wachovia’s losses]. By Sunday it was clear that [we would have to]. YPFS: You mentioned that you don't recall exactly who pitched the idea of the ring-fence. I'm curious if you have any recollection of the discussions leading up to that. One thing that Sheila Bair discussed is, if you have a class of bad assets—theoretically, that's what the Troubled Assets Relief Program (TARP) is for: you could buy the bad assets off the book. Not the FDIC, but the Treasury. What were the other options that the FDIC, at least internally, and perhaps in consultation with the Treasury, were considering? And how did you end up doing the ring-fence as opposed to an alternative? Jason Cave: We were bigger fans of the good bank-bad bank model, also taking out bad assets. The view was that if there were some toxic assets, take them out, use this money. The Treasury, and I think particularly the New York Fed, my sense always was they didn't think you'd get enough bang for the buck [if you simply bought bad assets from struggling banks]. Think about it from a leverage standpoint. Yeah, okay, fine. So, you got to use a dollar to take a dollar out. That dollar's gone. And again, we don't know how big this is going to be. We don't think we're going to be able to go to the well again [for more money from Congress]. We need to be able to take that Treasury dollar and get eight bucks out of it or something. Or even think about these guarantees that were never called upon. Unlimited. That was a big difference. It didn't mean that we disagreed that there was an issue with the assets. It was how to best really employ these [Treasury funds to address the losses on the assets]. Again, I think Sheila and FDIC felt that, yeah, your dollar might go further on those [loss guarantees], but if you don't get enough confidence [from the market in response to that measure], what's it get you? I think we did see a lot of times where we would come up with these plans and the market reaction was not good. You constantly had different views. At that point, I think our view was, let's get the assets out, let's use the money. At that point, we were dealing with a world where that wasn't where the government was going to go. So now, how do we get the best deal for the government? And so, we have the Citi and Wells bids, and really what we're doing at that time is we've got a handful of people that are looking at the two bids. [The bidders say], "We'll bid. We'll buy Wachovia, but we need this amount ring- fenced and we're willing to take X loss position and we want the government to take this.” And they're different [bids]: different pools, different assets, different tranching, different answers to, "When does the government come in?" So, all that sort of stuff, and again, we at the FDIC, we had least-cost tests.5 You had all these things that we had to make sure that if we were going to be brought in, we went with the deal that was going to be the least cost [to the Deposit Insurance Fund]. And so, the Citi deal did it. Again, very limited information. It's very back-of-the-envelope. “Okay, yeah, the Citi pool is bigger, but they're willing to share $39 billion of the losses and Wells is sharing less.” It turned out that Citi, for us, was going to be the best. There was, we talked about this too, this idea of, "Okay, well, who [will take the risk for the government]? Who's going to come in and what's the tranching on the US side?" At the FDIC, we really wanted the first loss tranche at Citi to be substantive. We came up with this idea that it should be like 110% of expected losses. There wasn't anything deep with that. Citi was like, "Well, that's not going to work." And so, we went back and forth. And all of a sudden, to make it work Treasury was going to take a $5 billion position to bridge our discomfort. I think it was through the Exchange Stabilization Fund (ESF), whatever they had there. They're like, "Fine, we'll go. We'll take the first. Not first loss, the second loss." Then the FDIC came in. There was that. YPFS: Something interesting has happened here, first with respect to the bondholders. The narrative of course is WaMu losses were imposed on bondholders, and then the next day, Wachovia bondholders wanted their money back inappropriately. There's no reason why they should get their money back on a ten-year credit. So how did you talk about the bondholders that weekend for Wachovia? Was there an idea that there would be any bail-in there, or was it just like this fear, look what happened when we imposed losses on WaMu, so we're not going to do that again? Jason Cave: Oh, yeah. It was very clear that there was no appetite to make bondholders, in any way, shape, or form, take losses in that situation. So, whether that was driven by the view of someone in the room of what happened with WaMu, or whether it was just viewed as that their credit base was just so much more hypersensitive, it was not happening. YPFS: Is that something that the FDIC was kind of pushing against? Jason Cave: At that point it was so quick, I don't even think we were. I'm just trying to remember. I don't remember us really sort of saying, "You know what? Let's let this one play out. Let's take these." I think we were, at that point, it was such a quick thing, our main issue was, whoa, wait a second. This is going to be the first time where we're sort of really on the hook in an open bank setup. Because again, this is all not closed. YPFS: This is a systemic risk exception.6 Jason Cave: This is a systemic risk exception, but we're now dealing with open bank assistance, which we were like, "Oh. We're not in that business anymore."7 It was more of, "How do we really make sure we are protected because this is a different animal?" YPFS: How early on that weekend did everybody agree the systemic risk exception was going to happen one way or the other? Jason Cave: I think once it was clear by Saturday that a private transaction was not going to happen, that it was pretty clear it had to be an exception. Because, think about it, once it was clear that Citi or Wells—and those are really the only ones in the game, JP was absorbing WaMu—once it was clear and there was no one else, and we knew that closing this place wasn't putting it through the WaMu transaction, it became clear that the only way to bridge this would have to be a systemic risk exception. And there was going to be some form of government exposure for an open bank deal, which was like you said. YPFS: I want to ask a question about that. When we get to Citi, we find it in the tranches of the ring-fence, you have the Fed taking the tail risk off the table, agreeing to finance some of that. During the Wachovia ring-fence, expected losses were under the $42 billion trigger. But losses theoretically could have run all the way up to $270 billion. And Sheila Bair says, "Well, we have to go get a credit line from the Treasury for this." Now, on your timing, the Treasury's operating with ESF at this point and the ESF in August of 2008 was only about $40 billion dollars. If the losses had been $100 billion, $200 billion, the ESF would've taken a hit, the Deposit Insurance Fund (DIF) would've taken a hit. Was there at any point an implicit understanding that since you had a credit line from the Treasury, the Treasury would be able to call on the Fed in the event of extreme and very unlikely losses? Jason Cave: Right, because once you start counting the dollars and saying, "Well, there's only this," then you've already lost the whole bet. It was really the sense that these sorts of times really bring in the full firepower of the Fed. But that's where that was. And that's right, the Fed did not try and get the ring-fences. At the end we didn't do the ring-fence because of Wells. I was all set to talk about the Fed coming in on that one. The Fed talked about that one but didn't come in on that one. And that was a wonderful moment of time [with Citi] when Ben Bernanke said, "We'll come in and take on the tail risk." And Scott Alvarez started to say, "I don't think we will use this." And Bernanke said, "Well, we're going to do it. We're not going to need to take losses because of all these others, but we're going to do it." It endeared me to Ben Bernanke for all time because that was a big move. YPFS: So, your view is the Citi ring-fence with Wachovia didn't play out, but if it had, there was at least an implicit understanding that the Fed would've been there if the Treasury had ended up having to take losses—or provide a credit line, at least, for the FDIC—to take losses of $80 billion, $100 billion, something like that? Jason Cave: We were hoping. YPFS: We see with the Citi ring-fence later that there's this risk-weighting regulatory capital relief. So, we have the Targeted Investment Program [TIP] and the regulatory capital relief. In our research thus far, we didn't see evidence of a discussion of risk-weighted asset regulatory capital relief with Wachovia. Was that on the table? Obviously, it didn't go through, but do you recall if that was on the table at all? I thought the Fed would've been the one providing that risk-weighted capital relief, and the Fed wasn't actually a party to this one, at least explicitly. I'm curious if that was in the calculus at all. Jason Cave: I don't remember, to be quite honest. I think so; it had to have been. Because for Citi to make it all work, it had to have been on the table. If it wasn't, Citi would've had to take the $300 billion still on its books and do it at a high-risk weight. You asked a very good question. I don’t recall it getting as much discussion [in the Wachovia case]. I don't recall a lot of discussion about—"Is this right? Why are you giving credit when they're taking a multiple of first losses?" It did not get that kind of discussion, but it might have been in the term sheet, I just don't remember. YPFS: Were Citi and Wells Fargo as buyers very focused on how this would impact their own capital ratios? Jason Cave: They must have been. I'm sure there's a term sheet that shows that that was kind of key. I'm sure. YPFS: It just isn't public? Jason Cave: Yeah. I'm sure there is. And now that I'm thinking about it, it must have been because they were still so capital conscious with all that stuff, that had to be part of the deal. It just doesn't jump out. YPFS: This will be my last question on Wachovia, so we have time to move on to the other two. There was some controversy about the idea that Citi's bid for Wachovia was really for Citi and not for Wachovia, in the sense the Citi wanted the domestic deposit base. Geithner, the New York Fed, and the Treasury team wanted the Citi transaction to go through, and then of course, ultimately it didn't. But my reading was that even Wachovia executives read this as, "Okay, well ring-fencing with Citi purchasing us is really more about Citi than it is about us." Was there a sense of that in the FDIC, that Citi's bid for Wachovia was really in order to provide Citi with a stable US deposit base? Jason Cave: One of the things that became very controversial...[it poisoned the well] and I think it's a strong phrase, but I think it's a fair phrase—it poisoned the well for many of the remaining government discussions, the feeling that we at the FDIC were not getting the full story. There were many other discussions going on that we should have been privy to, given that our fund was often called upon. And so, there was this view that discussions were going on with the New York Fed, and Citi, and other types that had that kind of information. We were not made aware of that, I think probably [based on] the view that that would just make us even more reluctant to do things. But once it became clear that there were all these other side discussions, it poisoned the well because we felt that we were getting the information last minute to limit our ability to really develop alternative choices. And that was a problem. And it is, I would say, for future people, a problem to be aware of. YPFS: And even as early as the Wachovia deal you were concerned about this? Jason Cave: That's where it really began. And I think there was some resentment towards the FDIC for closing WaMu rather than using our fund and doing other things that people thought that that kind of got the ball rolling on the crisis. So, you had a lot of that. But by [the time of Wachovia’s failure], it was pretty clear that we were all reluctantly doing these things, and sharing information. It was very spotty. YPFS: Was WaMu something the FDIC was able to do alone? Were there no discussions with the Treasury at that time? And did they push back? About the structure of the JPMorgan deal? Jason Cave: Oh, we had plenty of discussions with the Fed, and Treasury, and OCC, and Office of Thrift Supervision. There was pushback from Geithner, who was at the New York Fed at that time. It’s fair to say that he had concerns. Sort of— "What are you guys doing? Why not do a systemic risk exception? Why are you doing this?” That sort of thing. And the view was because we could do this thing [without the exception]. But you have to remember, with WaMu we had time. We knew things were going down. While things got bad quickly, we were already working with JPMorgan and others a good month ahead of time. After that TPG thing went bad, we were doing a lot.8 That was probably one of our best examples of getting in, talking to potential buyers, JP, getting a good sense of how this is going to go. That was probably as good as it got. I think we had probably a good month of what I'd call readiness. Still hoping for a good portion of that month that we wouldn't have to use it, but we at least had built that framework. And we didn't get that from other [problem banks coming our way]. And again, since we're being all honest with these things, I think the view was that because some of the other banks had the OCC and Fed as [primary regulators] they were not as willing to keep us involved in those discussions. It really put us at a disadvantage. And that difference, it was always just viewed as us being difficult. We never really felt like we were equal parties at the table, so to speak. And that began with Wachovia. YPFS: Moving on to Citi, can you tell us a bit about how Citi arrived at the Asset Guarantee Program, the ring-fence for Citi? Obviously, we have the background of Citi and Wachovia, so Citi had thought about this before. But, broadly, how did the FDIC, the Treasury, and the Fed all end up agreeing to do the ring-fencing arrangement with Citi? Jason Cave: I think there was even more unhappiness among team US government because after we had signed the Citi deal, all of a sudden the tax code changes, and Wells Fargo could do a deal without any government assistance. And that of course, angered Citi, and also some in the government because, "Wait a second, a deal's a deal." It's important just to note that then we did finally have TARP. So, we had the TARP, we had the Temporary Liquidity Guarantee Program (TLGP). The government was now fully in on these things. And so at least for the FDIC, we felt that we'd done our part. TLGP, this is a big thing for us, to be guaranteeing holding company debt when we were a deposit insurer, it was a big deal. Systemic risk, fine. We weren't excited about it, but it actually helped. It did unlock the frozen markets, and some would say TLGP was probably one of the more beneficial [programs the government implemented in the crisis]. We did that, we had the TARP. So, all of a sudden Citi kind of comes back up on the radar again, with the idea of, "It's not enough." And we say-“What do you mean it's not enough?" It's a structure thing. A whole bunch of Citi’s deposits are outside the US, which means the FDIC insurance doesn't pay, it's China, Japan. And the problem with those [guarantees] is, they're just not as full. The guarantees are a little weaker or not clear. And so that was a big part of it. And that goes back to what you were saying earlier. I think some people thought that's why Wachovia would've helped. It would've helped Citi have a greater domestic footing. So, these things all play together. The government was seeing some big moves out of Japan, I think particularly. But out of Asia in general, in terms of deposits beginning to run. And so, I think it was Ned Kelly, the chief financial officer at Citi, who put that back on the table. But again, I think this was one of those things that we felt there had already been a lot of discussions going on in the government before it got to our desk. And then all of a sudden, the idea was that what we had done with TLGP, with TARP, it wasn't enough; that Citi still needed help. If we'd just done TARP, we'd given them $25 billion like everybody else. We'd also guaranteed probably hundreds of billions of their debt [through the TLGP]. If this is still not enough, maybe we need to start taking real actions. Maybe we need to start looking at a resolution, a true restructuring. Because, at what point do you say—Enough's enough? And that was not viewed by others in the government seriously. It was viewed by Dugan or Geithner, as fanciful talk. YPFS: Can I just get you to expand on that? When you say a restructuring, I know there was mention of a good bank-bad bank model. Can you talk a little bit to the plans that the FDIC had in mind for Citi in terms of a restructuring? Jason Cave: So, restructuring through a good bank-bad bank was in our mind, an authentic old fashioned, type transaction, not like what Citi did. Not a press release saying—"We have this Citi Holdings and we're going to put things over here." We were thinking of a true type of transaction: we're taking bad assets, we're marking them [to market] (this was always going to be where the problem was) and they're not worth $100, they're worth $65, and this $35 is being covered by debt holders or investors. Once you started to talk about people taking losses, you lost Citi clearly, and also Treasury, Fed, and OCC. And it really became: who's going to take the hit? And in their mind, it was no one. In our mind, somebody should, and it's either going to be done through a resolution or some sort of a restructuring where debtholders all have to get real. And we were never able to bridge that. The FDIC's view was also, from a very parochial standpoint, this is not our problem. Because most of those deposits were outside of the US, those would take in a failure, in a liquidation resolution, the FDIC could do that, resolve the bank, have the bankruptcy court doing the rest of it, and not take losses. And again, these things are all connected. The thing that's causing the problems, outside of the US, the thing that to avoid that, the government wants everyone to come in and take losses, was also the same thing to say, "That's not our issue, and so why would we?" So that brought those issues together. And it makes sense that anybody that was like Sheila... That was going to be a problem anybody should have. Anybody from the FDIC that says, "Oh yeah," you wouldn't be doing right by the fund. Because the other thing that you have to understand that is really important is our management and stewardship of the fund. If we just went along with all those things and we said to the American Bankers Association, "Guess what? Pony it up." Don't forget the rest of the industry is sucking wind, and we're closing them left and right, and then we're going to say—"Yeah, but you have to pay." We'd have been crucified. We're just stewards of the fund. And you have to understand, we also were accountable to Congress for the management of the fund, but also to all these other institutions that would've had to pay for Citi's losses.9 YPFS: If I can just ask another question on the resolution proposal. The FDIC had a proposal for a good bank-bad bank, but a cross-jurisdictional resolution over the weekend would be very difficult. Would that have been feasible in a practical sense? Jason Cave: No. I mean, it would not have been. I would say what it really was a strategy of, we think debt holders at this point needed to start to become involved and take some losses, and so it began the process of, "Boy, we don't want to be here again" à la the resolution—that's for a whole other day if you really want to talk about it. But again, from the parochial [view], if we have an insured depository institution (IDI), a very large IDI [like] Citi, that we can put in resolution and if you just close it, then we can do this and not take losses. And so, it was important too for the rest of the government to understand according to Hoyle’s [i.e., according to the rules] that's what we should have done, and it could have been done. It's not like if we did that, the FDIC would be taking losses. But again, the view [at the Fed] was, [if you put Citi in resolution], the rest of the system burns down. The idea there was to at least understand that that's a big move for us to have to make. And so again, this Citi discussion would've been difficult for anybody. And from the other side [the Fed], where the folks that had truly the financial stability hat on [would have been] like, "Are you crazy?" And so, a lot of this tension that gets talked about, I think it would've been there regardless of who were in the seats. So, you had that. I mean the other thing too, that was really interesting, and Greg talked about the risk weight, and I told him, I said, "Nobody was bringing in Norah Barger [then head of capital policy at the Federal Reserve Board] or the experts to say, I don't think you can do that under the rules." I mean, these were times where that was all being suspended. I mean, just to show you how crazy this was, the FDIC’s compensation for doing these was preferred stock and they got to include that preferred stock in capital. The risk weight thing is cute. The capital's meant to absorb losses before us. So, when you think about that, all of [those other rules were] just suspended. YPFS: How important was the risk weighting to Citi when they came with the proposal for the ring-fence? Is the ring-fencing really about taking risk off from the assets, or is it about regulatory capital? And of course, it can be about both, but how important did it seem to Citi when they were coming to the government with the proposal to have that risk weighted regulatory capital relief? Jason Cave: It seemed very important to them to have the risk weighted capital relief. I think, and I think others would agree, that the real value was showing that the government was standing behind them—not only just that it's in on TLGP and TARP but to show that it's in even more. I think the reality was to tell them, and to everybody else, "Don't worry." YPFS: It was a signaling effect? Jason Cave: I think the real value was look, I mean, it was not so much that [Citi’s leadership was thinking,] "We're so bad, they have to be in," but "We're so important that they're not going to let us fail." I think that was the whole ball of wax. But I will say that that was always very important [to them] to get this risk weight. I never bought it for a second. YPFS: Another thing that we were talking about this morning was why not just nationalize them like we did with AIG, and like the Brits did with several large banks? It reassures the liability holders. Jason Cave: Yeah, I mean, look, with the government-sponsored enterprises, we didn't take three times with them [like we did with Citi]. YPFS: You didn't mess with that. Jason Cave: Some have said, "It didn't take a whole lot to go that route." YPFS: Nationalizing means you're wiping out shareholders. It means people are losing their jobs. It could be spun as something which addresses moral hazard rather than creates it. Did that not come up? Jason Cave: I am sure it came up, and again, I wasn't a principal. I was close to a lot of discussions, but I was never in any discussions where nationalization was seriously discussed. I mean, that just shows you what a third rail issue it is. I'm sure it might've come up, but it was not encouraged. YPFS: What's the difference between Citi and AIG and Fannie? Jason Cave: That is a great question. And the other great thing with this is as I tell people too, I went to work at the Federal Housing Finance Agency after I left FDIC, and they talk about conservatorship, and they're like, "Well, you must know this." [My response to my FHFA colleagues was] "I got to tell you, once you guys went down that road, and did that, I didn't have time to think of anything but banks [since I was still at the FDIC], not even AIG." All I knew about AIG was [Federal Reserve official] Sarah Dahlgren's got it covered.10 It was tunnel [vision]: we have this thing in front of us [to focus on]. At least for me. But they're good questions. Why did we do it that way? Why was nationalization not a serious option? It wasn't. It wasn't like, "We have a ring- fence or nationalization, let's work them both through." At least in meetings I was in, that wasn't the case. Maybe in some other places it was, but it really wasn't. YPFS: But to go back to that, what were the options? If the FDIC was opposed to the ring-fence, and I believe Sheila Bair says in her book, "We didn't think this was super credible, that the ring-fence by itself would do a lot anyways." What were the main alternatives being considered? Jason Cave: She [Sheila Bair] was back to taking assets out again. At that point, the view was—, "Wait a second, if TARP's not enough, if TLGP's not enough, the market's telling us you've got to get the assets out."— at least with Citi. So, at that point, we had these public partnership type things, taking assets out, having structures where other market people shared in the upside, some of that stuff. But she really was pushing that, because she's saying, "The market's telling us, and all you guys"—meaning Citi and the others in the government— "are coming up with, once again, something that we can do on the cheap. But that's not going to work." And so that became a real point of discussion of: "I'm not going to do this unless we seriously consider a true good bank-bad bank where, again, if we're going to have marks, let's use the capital for that." That was the point. It's like, "Okay, we know they're not going to, and okay, fine. If we're not going to have creditors [take losses], fine. But let's get these assets marked and use the capital for that." But once again, it's like every dollar for that, there's a dollar there, and we can't get the full amount. So, it was this continued theme. YPFS: We know that coterminous with the ring-fencing arrangement, there was the TIP with more capital coming in from the Treasury. Was there any point in this weekend of these ring-fence discussions, of just saying, "What they need is common equity"? We see months later that the market seems to be discounting regulatory capital and saying that Citi needs common equity. Was more common equity on the table on Citi weekend? Jason Cave: There was, and I'm trying to remember why. First off, you're right. And again, the answer is that's what is needed, the market's saying it. I'm trying to remember legally if we couldn't use TARP for common equity. It definitely was talked about, and it was dismissed. I think I remember Paulson was opposed to it; I think because of concerns about nationalization. That's what it was. YPFS: I believe the reason Treasury chose preferred shares for TIP was because it was a control issue. Jason Cave: That's what it was. Yes. YPFS: I don't think that it was a legal issue because they later converted some preferred shares to common. Jason Cave: Oh, yeah, I remember that deal, too. But we were very frustrated on that part because that was Citi part three, wasn't it? Or four? I lose track. YPFS: Was that post Supervisory Capital Assessment Program [SCAP] or was it before? Jason Cave: It was before SCAP. SCAP kind of fixed everything. We all remember that footnote, but anyhow.11 But just on that one. Again, what was driving the FDIC crazy was when all of a sudden it still wasn't enough and the government had to convert to common equity. We had made the case that we should be making the trust preferred holders that are pari passu with us also convert. YPFS: That was a question we had: What was going on with the trust preferreds? Why did those not convert? Jason Cave: I was always a big skeptic of trust preferred. When people would say, "Oh, well, if you need it, you can do it." I had made the case to Sheila that if we're going to do this, this stuff's pari passu—we should insist that the [existing] trust preferreds also convert [to common equity] alongside of [Treasury’s and the FDIC’s trust preferreds]. It made perfect sense. First off, that's what they're supposed to do. You would've thought we were asking for the sisters of the charity to put money in. It was such a big deal. But finally, we got something, I forget exactly what, but to me, it was the clearest thing to show that your government is not just out there taking all these things, that we've got private investors taking risks too. But it was such a challenge to get. YPFS: So that was confirming that the preferred that the FDIC received were not junior to the existing trust preferred. Is that what it was doing? Jason Cave: Yes. Yeah. But it was like, "Why would we not do this at this point to have some of the private investors share in this?" And it was so difficult. When we raised it, I thought this was a no-brainer. It just showed you the risk tolerance for anybody in the private side taking any hits, even though at Fannie and Freddie we liquidated. YPFS: To bring it back to the ring-fence, can we talk a bit about how the Fed ended up coming in to take the tail risk position? We know that the Fed expected that Citi losses wouldn't even approach the amount at which it would need to lend, so then why even do it at all? Was it really valuable to take that tail risk off? Another idea is that it allowed the Fed to do the risk weight changes, because of the supervisors and regulators. Or it could have been a signaling communication strategy. What was your recollection of how the Fed got involved in taking the tail risk and financing that last tranche? Jason Cave: From what I remember being in the discussions with the principals, it was really this issue of, once again, the FDIC saying, "We're the last ones being brought into the discussions, we’re the first ones taking the losses after Citi's first loss, and we don't think that their first loss piece is big enough. But also, we haven't had nearly as much time to analyze the portfolio; we don't like capital support for banks that needed it, potentially including Citigroup. See page 17 and Footnote 12 of “*The Supervisory Capital Assessment Program: Design and Implementation (federalreserve.gov) and “Inside Citi's Stress Test: More like an F than a B+”, TIME https://time.com/archive/6905967/inside-citis-stress-test- more-like-an-f-than-a-b/ being brought in late and then being the first ones taking it.” So [there was] that resistance [from the FDIC]. So, then Treasury is saying, "Well, fine. We'll take that first tranche and then you come in." There was just a lot of angst going on, and I remember it. And Ben Bernanke said, "We'll come in and do a non-recourse loan on the tail." And it was not a risk weight thing, it was a good sign we're all in this. YPFS: So, it had nothing to do with the risk weighting? The Fed did not need to be involved to provide the risk weighting? Jason Cave: No. It was that "We're all in this," and I remember Scott Alvarez and others saying, "Well, I'm not sure." Because it was non-recourse at that time—where everything's non-recourse—and I think the view was, "We're not going to take losses anyway, so whatever." YPFS: So, your recollection is there was some legal controversy over the Fed providing the contingent loan facility? Jason Cave: Oh, yeah. I remember where I was in my house when the discussion happened. This was a big deal. Alvarez was also being a very good lawyer, and up to the moment where that was said, he had kept the Fed off that. Even if they could legally, he was doing just what he should do of saying, "Wait a second, we're at the last minute of this thing." And so, he was doing what a good lawyer should do. YPFS: So, were the other government agencies, the FDIC and the Treasury, requesting that the Fed come in? Or was the Fed a party to these discussions and said, "Look, stop the infighting. We'll take off the tail risk"? But they likely wouldn't have lent anyways, so would that have helped comfort the FDIC or the Treasury? Jason Cave: It did help. And I don't remember if we asked them: there were a lot of discussions going on while other things were going on. But I remember it more like, "Let's all just be here together." And it helped. Again, financially, did it change anything? No, but it just helped. YPFS: With the focus on the tail risk, the market's point of view seemed to be that Citi could lose $50 billion or $60 billion on this portfolio. The Fed's consultants said it would be no more than $30 billion or $40 billion, and it ended up being $10 billion. How were estimates so different? Jason Cave: Part of it is that the numbers get out of whack when nobody knows what the hell you're ring-fencing either. YPFS: Because that weekend they hadn't said which assets they were going to put in the ring fence? Jason Cave: Only broad categories: "Oh, there'll be a little of this or that." And then it was changed. The real crazy thing was that you never really knew what it was. And then we found out that they had some foreign stuff in the mix, and then somebody in legal goes, "Actually, the TARP can't fund that stuff." There were all these things included and then some smart lawyers said, "The TARP can't fund that." So okay, well, that has to go. "Well, we'll put this in." Okay. And the more detail you've got, things either were not legally able to be in there if they had a TARP thing, or they weren't sure. It was a mess. So, part of it was, yeah, the losses were a lot less because nobody knew what we were even covering. YPFS: It's a difference. If you say to the market, "Citi's still going to bear the first $40 billion, but the government's here to bear the next $15 billion," it doesn't sound like much. But if you say the government's here to guarantee everything after that, it just sounds a lot different, even though nobody in the room thought that the losses would be that big. Jason Cave: Yeah. Nobody was really going through all of that. YPFS: It seems very unscientific in retrospect. Jason Cave: Very unscientific. Nobody was sitting there like, "Okay, well, if it's a $50 billion loss and then the Fed's in for this and then the shareholders... but then the shareholders are also really TARP, so that's Treasury."
